facts.statement: Dryornis, meaning "tree bird" and also known as the Argentinian vulture, is an extinct genus of New World vulture from the early Miocene to early Pliocene of Argentina.
facts.quote: Dryornis (meaning "tree bird"), also called the Argentinian vulture, is an extinct genus of cathartid (New World vulture) known from the early Miocene–early Pliocene of Argentina.

facts.statement: The genus Dryornis was first described in 1891 by Argentine paleontologists Francisco Moreno and Alcides Mercerat.
facts.quote: Dryornis was first described in 1891 by Argentine paleontologists Francisco Moreno and Alcides Mercerat

facts.statement: The type species Dryornis pampeanus was originally based on a right humerus and a right femur.
facts.quote: The type species being D. pampeanus, based on the distal portion of a right humerus and a right femur

facts.statement: The species Dryornis hatcheri was described in 2022 by Federico J. Degrange after it remained unstudied since its initial discovery.
facts.quote: It remained unstudied until 2022, when Argentine paleontologist Federico J. Degrange noticed its true affinities and described it as a new species of Dryornis, D. hatcheri.

facts.statement: The original fossils of Dryornis were collected from the Pliocene-age Monte Hermoso Formation in Buenos Aires, Argentina.
facts.quote: The fossils had been collected from the Pliocene age deposits of the Monte Hermoso Formation in Buenos Aires, Argentina

facts.statement: Fossils from the La Estafeta Beach in Mar del Plata allowed detailed phylogenetic analysis and revealed new diagnostic characteristics for Dryornis pampeanus.
facts.quote: The fossils allowed more detailed analysis of the species' phylogeny and revealed many novel diagnostic characteristics for the species.

facts.statement: Dryornis is the largest known cathartiform bird, excluding the Teratornithidae family.
facts.quote: Dryornis represents the largest known cathartiform other than the Teratornithidae.

facts.statement: Analysis of fossils suggests Dryornis had a body mass of 26 kg.
facts.quote: Analysis of the known fossil materials suggests that it had a body mass of 26 kg

facts.statement: The wingspan of Dryornis pampeanus was likely between 3.87 and 4 meters.
facts.quote: The wingspan of Dryornis pampeanus was likely between 3.87 - 4 m.

facts.statement: Dryornis is distinguished by a highly pneumatized sternum, likely an adaptation for its large size and flight.
facts.quote: One feature distinguishing Dryornis from other cathartids is the presence of a much more pneumatized sternum, likely an adaptation for its size and flight capabilities.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses place Dryornis within the family Cathartidae as a sister taxon to Coragyps and Cathartes.
facts.quote: In their phylogenetic analyses, Degrange et al. (2021) recovered Dryornis as a member of the Cathartidae and sister taxon to Coragyps+Cathartes.

facts.statement: Dryornis lived from the Aquitanian to the Zanclean stages, approximately 23.04 to 3.8 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aquitanian to Zanclean (23.04 to 3.8 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Dryornis was a scavenger and the only scavenging predator in its ecosystem.
rejected.quote: Dryornis would have been a scavenger, and the only such predator in its ecosystem.
